units.unit: Wants to see the working paper estimating supply elasticity and modelling a tightened cap
Wants the NGO survey of subdivided-unit tenants
Core claim needing backing: a hard cap on initial rents would shrink stock rather than help tenants
Needs the modelling paper to show how much stock a cap-induced rent cut removes and who bears it
Tenant survey can wait
Needs supply elasticity modelling paper for the core claim
Wants enforcement, tenant survey, Berlin case, and stock index too
Worked backwards from evidence rather than starting with a policy
Elasticity findings and failure of hard caps told him what not to do
Tenant survey plus Mr Chan's answer told him what tenants actually want
Three-part package is what was left once alternatives were ruled out
Consultation source floating a floor-standard plus rent band gave the specific shape
Figure came from D6p1, long-run elasticity of SDU-type supply estimated at 0.31 to 0.48
Hadn't used that source earlier, so the point is new to the essay
Brought it in because the supply-elasticity estimate is core economic evidence that a binding cap would shrink marginal stock
Number came from own calculation multiplying the 0.31 to 0.48 elasticity by the 10 percent rent cut
Should have shown the arithmetic in the paragraph rather than presenting the result as stated in the source
Built the sentence from the working paper's modelling of a tightened cap in a Hong Kong-like market at D6p4
Treated the 15 percent scenario as the paper's illustration, not his own calculation, since he had already taken the elasticity from D6p1
Put it in paragraph 3 because it was the clearest numbers for the trade-off between helping current tenants and shutting out new ones
Got the distinction from D6p2, first-generation hard caps on levels versus second-generation caps on increases
Used it to re-read the 2021 ordinance as a second-generation instrument
Stable stock in D2p1 doesn't prove a harder cap is safe
Point came out of comparing those two sources, not from outside
